pairs.source_text: Synthesibus dum gaudet eques dominusque senator Dumque decent nostrum pillea sumpta Iovem;
pairs.question: Qua veste Saturnalibus etiam eques et senator gaudere dicuntur apud Martialem in Apophoretis?
pairs.question_en: In what garment do even the knight and the senator rejoice at the Saturnalia, according to Martial in the Apophoreta?
pairs.derivation: The proem of the Apophoreta: during the Saturnalia the toga was laid aside and everyone, up to knights and senators, wore the informal synthesis; the pilleus (freedom-cap) was likewise worn. The Saturnalian frame is explicit in the poem (v. 9 'madidis, Saturne, diebus'). Anchored to Martial + Saturnalia; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec timet aedilem moto spectare fritillo, Cum videat gelidos tam prope verna lacus:
pairs.question: Quem magistratum aleator, moto fritillo, Saturnalibus non timet, ut scribit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Which magistrate does the dicer, rattling his dice-box, not fear during the Saturnalia, as Martial writes?
pairs.derivation: Gambling with dice was normally policed by the aediles, but the ban was suspended during the Saturnalia — the classic 'Saturnalian license' fact, stated in the proem. Anchored to the fritillo/Saturnalia frame; single-office answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Divitis alternas et pauperis accipe sortes: Praemia convivae dent sua quisque suo.
pairs.question: Quorum duorum hominum sortes alternae in Apophoretis Martialis leguntur?
pairs.question_en: Whose alternating lots are read in Martial's Apophoreta?
pairs.answer_en: The rich man's and the poor man's.
pairs.derivation: The organizing frame of the whole book, stated in the proem: the gift-couplets alternate between a rich man's present and a poor man's, to be drawn by lot (sortes) at the Saturnalian banquet. Anchored to the Apophoreta by name; two-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quo vis cumque loco potes hunc finire libellum: Versibus explicitumst omne duobus opus.
pairs.question: Quot versibus unumquodque munus in Apophoretis Martialis explicatur?
pairs.question_en: In how many verses is each gift treated in Martial's Apophoreta?
pairs.derivation: The book states its own form: every item is complete in a two-line epigram, so the reader may stop anywhere (and, the poem adds, may read the lemmata alone). Anchored to the Apophoreta; single-number answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Secta nisi in tenues essemus ligna tabellas, Essemus Libyci nobile dentis onus.
pairs.question: Quo sustinebantur mensae citreae pretiosae apud Romanos, ut innuit Martialis de pugillaribus citreis?
pairs.question_en: On what did the costly citrus-wood tables rest among the Romans, as Martial hints in the couplet on citrus-wood tablets?
pairs.derivation: The famous luxury pairing: tabletops of African citrus wood rested on legs of elephant ivory — had the wood not been cut into humble tablets, it would have been 'the noble burden of the Libyan tusk.' Anchored to the citrus-wood object; short answer supported verbatim (Libyci dentis onus).

pairs.source_text: Esse puta ceras, licet haec membrana vocetur: Delebis, quotiens scripta novare voles.
pairs.question: Quid in pugillaribus membraneis facere licet, quotiens scripta novare velis, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What may one do on parchment tablets whenever one wishes to renew what is written, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Parchment notebooks (pugillares membranei) could be wiped and reused like wax tablets — a key fact of Roman writing culture and of the early history of parchment. Anchored to the named object; short answer supported verbatim (Delebis... novare voles).

pairs.source_text: Nondum legerit hos licet puella, Novit quid cupiant Vitelliani.
pairs.question: Quo nomine vocabantur pugillares illi quos amantes ad blanditias mittere solebant, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: By what name were called the little tablets that lovers used to send for their sweet nothings, as Martial jokes?
pairs.derivation: Vitelliani were small writing-tablets proverbially used for love-notes — a girl knows what they want before she even reads them. A named object of daily life; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hos nisi de flava loculos implere moneta Non decet: argentum vilia ligna ferant.
pairs.question: Qua moneta loculos eboreos impleri decere scribit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: With what coin does Martial write that ivory money-boxes should be filled?
pairs.derivation: The decorum of containers: ivory caskets are for gold coin, cheap wooden ones may carry silver. Anchored to the named object (loculi eborei); short answer supported verbatim (de flava moneta).

pairs.source_text: Cum steterit nullus vultu tibi talus eodem, Munera me dices magna dedisse tibi.
pairs.question: Quis iactus in ludo talorum optimus habetur, teste Martiale in Apophoretis?
pairs.answer: Cum nullus talus eodem vultu stat.
pairs.question_en: Which throw is held the best in the game of knucklebones, on Martial's testimony in the Apophoreta?
pairs.answer_en: When no knucklebone lands showing the same face (all four different).
pairs.derivation: The winning throw at tali — all four knucklebones showing different faces (the 'Venus' throw) — is stated as the moment the gift proves great. A core fact of Roman gaming culture; answer supported verbatim (nullus vultu talus eodem).

pairs.source_text: Non sim talorum numero par tessera, dum sit Maior, quam talis, alea saepe mihi.
pairs.question: Utro ludo maior alea fieri solet, tesseris an talis, secundum Martialem?
pairs.question_en: In which game do the stakes usually run higher, dice (tesserae) or knucklebones (tali), according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: The two Roman dice-games distinguished: the tesserae are fewer in number than the tali but carry the bigger gamble (maior alea). Anchored to the two named game-pieces; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quae scit compositos manus improba mittere talos, Si per me misit, nil nisi vota feret.
pairs.question: Ad quid turricula in ludo talorum adhibebatur, teste Martiale?
pairs.answer: Ne manus improba compositos talos mitteret.
pairs.question_en: For what purpose was the turricula (dice-tower) used in the game of knucklebones, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: So that a cheating hand could not throw 'arranged' knucklebones (to prevent cheating).
pairs.derivation: The dice-tower (turricula, the lemma of the epigram) randomizes the throw: a hand skilled at slipping in a fixed cast wins nothing if it must throw through the tower. A concrete fact of Roman gaming equipment; answer supported verbatim by the couplet.

pairs.source_text: Hac mihi bis seno numeratur tessera puncto; Calculus hac gemino discolor hoste perit.
pairs.question: Quot hostibus oppressus calculus in ludo latrunculorum perit, ut scribit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: By how many enemies is a piece taken (destroyed) in the game of latrunculi, as Martial writes?
pairs.derivation: The capture rule of latrunculi: a piece perishes when caught by two enemy pieces (custodia capture) — stated on the game-board couplet. A core rule of the most popular Roman board game; number answer supported verbatim (gemino hoste perit).

pairs.source_text: Hac mihi bis seno numeratur tessera puncto; Calculus hac gemino discolor hoste perit.
pairs.question: Quot punctis tessera in altera parte tabulae lusoriae numeratur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: With how many points is the die counted on the one side of the gaming-board in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: With twice six points (twelve) — the 'twelve lines' game.
pairs.derivation: The tabula lusoria was double-sided: one face for the dice game of 'twelve points' (duodecim scripta), the other for latrunculi. The number bis seno puncto is stated verbatim; anchored to the named gaming-board.

pairs.source_text: Insidiosorum si ludis bella latronum, Gemmeus iste tibi miles et hostis erit.
pairs.question: Quorum bella ludo calculorum luduntur, ut ait Martialis in Apophoretis?
pairs.question_en: Whose wars are played in the game of gaming-pieces (calculi), as Martial says in the Apophoreta?
pairs.answer_en: Those of the ambushing 'robbers' (latrones) — it is a war-game of soldiers.
pairs.derivation: Latrunculi was conceived as a battle of 'latrones' (soldiers/brigands), the piece serving as both one's soldier and the foe's; here the gift pieces are of gemstone/glass. Anchored to the named game; short answer supported verbatim (bella latronum).

pairs.source_text: Alea parva nuces et non damnosa videtur; Saepe tamen pueris abstulit illa natis.
pairs.question: Quae alea parva nec damnosa pueris esse videtur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What is regarded as a small and harmless gamble for boys in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Nuts were the proverbial small-stakes gambling of children, especially at the Saturnalia (cf. the proem's 'Lude nucibus'). Anchored to the named stake; one-word answer supported verbatim (Alea parva nuces).

pairs.source_text: Sortitus thecam calamis armare memento: Cetera nos dedimus, tu leviora para.
pairs.question: Quibus instrumentis thecam librariam armare debet qui eam sortitus est, ut monet Martialis?
pairs.question_en: With what implements must the man who has drawn a writing-case arm it, as Martial advises?
pairs.derivation: The theca libraria was the case for one's reed pens — the winner of the lot must furnish the calami himself. A named object of Roman writing culture; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Haec tibi erunt armata suo graphiaria ferro: Si puero dones, non leve munus erit.
pairs.question: Quo armatum est graphiarium apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: With what is the stylus-case (graphiarium) armed in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The graphiarium held the iron styli for writing on wax — Martial adds it makes no slight gift for a schoolboy. A named object of writing culture; answer supported verbatim (armata suo ferro).

pairs.source_text: Lentiscum melius: sed si tibi frondea cuspis Defuerit, dentes pinna levare potest.
pairs.question: Quae materia dentiscalpio optima habetur secundum Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What material is held best for a toothpick according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: The canonical Roman toothpick was a sliver of mastic (lentiscus); failing that, a quill (pinna) would do. Anchored to the named implement; one-word answer supported verbatim (Lentiscum melius).

pairs.source_text: Splendida ne madidi violent bombycina crines, Figat acus tortas sustineatque comas.
pairs.question: Quid agit acus aurea in cultu mulieris Romanae, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What does the golden hairpin do in a Roman woman's toilette, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: It pins and holds up the twisted (piled) hair.
pairs.derivation: The acus (hairpin) fixed the elaborate piled coiffure so that perfumed hair would not stain the silk (bombycina) garments. A named toilette object of daily life; answer supported verbatim (figat acus tortas sustineatque comas).

pairs.source_text: Chattica Teutonicos accendit spuma capillos: Captivis poteris cultior esse comis.
pairs.question: Ex quibus comis capillamenta sua mulieres Romanae parare poterant, ut ait Martialis in Apophoretis?
pairs.question_en: From whose hair could Roman women furnish their wigs, as Martial says in the Apophoreta?
pairs.answer_en: From the captive hair of the Germans.
pairs.derivation: Blond German hair — here 'Teutonic' locks brightened by Chattian soap-foam — was taken from captives and worn at Rome as wigs (crines, the lemma). A famous fact of Roman fashion; answer supported verbatim (Captivis... comis, Teutonicos capillos).

pairs.source_text: Si mutare paras longaevos cana capillos, Accipe Mattiacas - quo tibi calva? - pilas.
pairs.question: Quibus pilis mulier cana capillos mutare (tinguere) potest secundum Martialem?
pairs.question_en: With what balls can a grey-haired woman change (dye) her hair, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: Sapo (the lemma): the German soap-balls from Mattiacum (near Wiesbaden) used at Rome as hair-dye for greying hair. Named product + named origin; answer supported verbatim (Mattiacas... pilas).

pairs.source_text: In Pompeiano tecum spectabo theatro: Mandatus populo vela negare solet.
pairs.question: Quid populo in theatro Pompeiano ventus negare solet, ut ait Martialis de causea?
pairs.question_en: What does the wind usually deny the people in the theater of Pompey, as Martial says of the causea (spectator's hat)?
pairs.derivation: The great theaters were shaded by vela (awnings), but wind could force them to stay furled — hence the causea, a broad hat, as spectator's gear. Anchored to the theater of Pompey; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Excipient apros expectabuntque leones, Intrabunt ursos, sit modo firma manus.
pairs.question: Quas tres feras venabula excipere et intrare parata sunt apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What three beasts are hunting-spears ready to receive and pierce in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The canonical big game of the Roman hunt (venatio), listed on the gift of venabula. Anchored to the named weapon; three-noun answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si deiecta gemas longo venabula rostro, Hic brevis ingentem comminus ibit aprum.
pairs.question: Quam feram culter venatorius comminus adire dicitur, si venabula deiecta sunt, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What beast is the hunting-knife said to go against at close quarters when the spears have been struck down, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The culter venatorius was the hunter's short close-quarters blade against the boar, backup when the boar's snout beat down the long spear. Anchored to the named implement; one-word answer supported verbatim (comminus ibit aprum).

pairs.source_text: Militiae decus hoc gratique erit omen honoris, Arma tribunicium cingere digna latus.
pairs.question: Cuius officii militaris latus cingere digna sunt arma quae parazonium vocantur, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: The side of what military officer are the arms called parazonium worthy to gird, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The parazonium (the lemma), a short sword worn as a badge of rank, befits the military tribune — an omen of the office to come. Anchored to the named object; short answer supported verbatim (tribunicium... latus).

pairs.source_text: Pugio, quem curva signat brevis orbita vena. Stridentem gelidis hunc Salo tinxit aquis.
pairs.question: Quod flumen pugionem stridentem gelidis aquis tinxisse dicit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What river does Martial say tempered the hissing dagger in its cold waters?
pairs.answer_en: The Salo (the river of Bilbilis in Spain).
pairs.derivation: The Salo, the river of Martial's native Bilbilis in Hispania, was famed for tempering steel — blades were quenched hissing in its cold water. Named river + named weapon; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Pax me certa ducis placidos curvavit in usus. Agricolae nunc sum, militis ante fui.
pairs.question: Cuius fuit ante falx illa quae nunc agricolae est, ut loquitur ipsa apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Whose was the sickle before, which now belongs to the farmer, as it says of itself in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The famous sword-beaten-into-sickle couplet: the emperor's assured peace bent the soldier's blade to the farmer's peaceful use. Anchored to the falx (the lemma) speaking of itself; one-word answer supported verbatim (militis ante fui).

pairs.source_text: Tondendis haec arma tibi sunt apta capillis; Unguibus hic longis utilis, illa genis.
pairs.question: Quibus tribus usibus ferramenta tonsoria apta sunt apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: For what three uses is the barber's kit of irons fitted in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: For cutting hair, for the (long) nails, and for the cheeks (shaving).
pairs.derivation: The Roman barber (tonsor) cut hair, pared nails, and shaved cheeks — the three services named on the gift of ferramenta tonsoria. Anchored to the named kit; three-item answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dat chartis habiles calamos Memphitica tellus; Texantur reliqua tecta palude tibi.
pairs.question: Quae terra calamos chartis habiles dare dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What land is said to supply the reed pens suited for writing on papyrus, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Writing reeds, like the papyrus itself, came from the Egyptian marshes — 'the land of Memphis' supplies the calami fit for chartae. Named place + named implement; answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dulcis conscia lectuli lucerna, Quidquid vis facias licet, tacebo.
pairs.question: Quid promittit lucerna cubicularis, conscia lectuli, apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What does the bedroom lamp, confidant of the bed, promise in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated couplet on the lucerna cubicularis: the lamp that witnesses everything done in the bedroom and promises silence ('tacebo'). Anchored to the named object; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Inlustrem cum tota meis convivia flammis Totque geram myxos, una lucerna vocor.
pairs.question: Quid gerit lucerna quae polymyxos vocatur, ut ipsa loquitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What does the lamp called polymyxos carry, as it says of itself in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The lucerna polymyxos (the lemma) is the many-wicked lamp that can light a whole banquet by itself though called a single lamp. Anchored to the named lamp-type; short answer supported verbatim (totque geram myxos).

pairs.source_text: Nomina candelae nobis antiqua dederunt: Non norat parcos uncta lucerna patres.
pairs.question: Quo lumine parci patres Romanorum antiqui utebantur, cum lucernam unctam nondum nossent, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What light did the frugal Roman forefathers use, when they did not yet know the oil lamp, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: On the Corinthian candelabrum: it takes its ancient name from the candela, because the oil lamp was unknown to the thrifty ancestors — a fact of early Roman domestic history. Anchored to the maiores; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Haec quae difficili turget paganica pluma, Folle minus laxast et minus arta pila.
pairs.question: Qua re farta turget pila paganica apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: With what stuffing does the paganica ball bulge in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The paganica, the 'countryman's ball,' was stuffed hard with feathers. Anchored to the named ball-type of the Roman game taxonomy; one-word answer supported verbatim (turget paganica pluma).

pairs.source_text: Haec quae difficili turget paganica pluma, Folle minus laxast et minus arta pila.
pairs.question: Inter quas duas pilas media est paganica mollitie sua, ut docet Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Between which two balls does the paganica stand midway in its softness, as Martial teaches?
pairs.answer_en: Between the follis (air-ball) and the (hard) pila.
pairs.derivation: The Roman ball taxonomy in one line: the paganica is less slack than the inflated follis and less hard-packed than the pila proper. Anchored to the three named ball types; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si me nobilibus scis expulsare sinistris, Sum tua. Tu nescis? rustice, redde pilam.
pairs.question: Qua manu peritus lusor pilam trigonalem expulsare scit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: With which hand does the skilled player know how to strike back the trigon ball, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: In the trigon (three-corner ball game), the mark of the expert was returning the ball with elegant left-handed strokes (nobilibus sinistris); the duffer must give the ball back. Anchored to the named game; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ite procul, iuvenes: mitis mihi convenit aetas: Folle decet pueros ludere, folle senes.
pairs.question: Quas aetates folle ludere decet secundum Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What ages is it fitting to play with the follis (air-filled ball), according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: The follis, the light inflated ball, was the gentle game for the two mild ages — boys and old men — while young men are sent away. Anchored to the named ball; two-word answer supported verbatim (Folle decet pueros ludere, folle senes).

pairs.source_text: Haec rapit Antaei velox in pulvere draucus, Grandia qui vano colla labore facit.
pairs.question: Quo in loco harpasta rapi solent apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Where are the harpasta (snatch-balls) usually snatched, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The harpastum was the snatching ball-game played on the dusty wrestling-ground ('the dust of Antaeus') by muscle-building athletes — completing the ball-game taxonomy. Anchored to the named game; short answer supported verbatim (rapit... in pulvere).

pairs.source_text: Ne lutet inmundum nitidos ceroma capillos, Hac poteris madidas condere pelle comas.
pairs.question: A qua re galericulum comas athletae defendit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: From what does the little leather cap (galericulum) protect the athlete's hair, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: From the ceroma (the wrestler's mud-and-oil ointment).
pairs.derivation: The galericulum (the lemma), a skin cap, kept the filthy ceroma of the wrestling-ground from fouling well-kept hair. Two named objects of Roman athletics; answer supported verbatim (Ne lutet inmundum... ceroma capillos... pelle).

pairs.source_text: Pergamon has misit. Curvo destringere ferro: Non tam saepe teret lintea fullo tibi.
pairs.question: Quae urbs strigiles Romam misisse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What city is said to have sent the strigils to Rome, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Strigils — the curved iron scrapers of the baths — came from Pergamon; scraping with them spares one's linen towels from the fuller. Named city + named implement; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nuper in Ausonia domini spectatus harena Hic erit ille tibi, cui pila taurus erat.
pairs.question: Quod animal, nuper in harena domini spectatum, taurum quasi pilam iactabat, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What animal, lately exhibited in the emperor's arena, tossed a bull about as if it were a ball, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The rhinoceros (the lemma; here a flask of its horn) exhibited in Domitian's amphitheater famously tossed a bull like a ball — the same show celebrated in Martial's Liber spectaculorum. Anchored to the emperor's arena; one-word answer supported by the lemma + couplet (cui pila taurus erat).

pairs.source_text: Proficies nihil hoc, caedas licet usque, flagello, Si tibi purpureo de grege currit equus.
pairs.question: De quo grege currit equus circensis cui flagellum nihil proficiet, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: From what stable does the race-horse run for which the whip will do no good, as Martial jokes?
pairs.answer_en: From the purple stable (the purple faction).
pairs.derivation: Evidence for the purple racing faction (purpureus grex) of the circus, added under Domitian alongside the old colors — the horse from that stable needs no whip. Anchored to the flagellum gift + the named faction color; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid mecum est tibi? me puella sumat: Emptos non soleo polire dentes.
pairs.question: Quales dentes dentifricium polire non solere ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What sort of teeth does tooth-powder say it does not polish, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: The dentifricium jokes that it will not polish purchased teeth — Roman evidence for false teeth (cf. Martial's Laecania). A daily-life fact anchored to the named product; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Balsama me capiunt, haec sunt unguenta virorum: Delicias Cosmi vos redolete, nurus.
pairs.question: Quae unguenta virorum propria esse dicit Martialis in Apophoretis?
pairs.question_en: Which perfume does Martial in the Apophoreta declare the proper scent of men?
pairs.derivation: The gendering of Roman perfume: plain balsam for men, while the confections of Cosmus — the most famous perfumer of Rome — are left to young women. Anchored to the named unguent; one-word answer supported verbatim (haec sunt unguenta virorum).

pairs.source_text: Gratum munus erit scisso nec inutile ventri, Si clara Stephani balnea luce petes.
pairs.question: Cui corporis parti lomentum gratum et utile est, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: For what part of the body is bean-meal paste (lomentum) a welcome and useful gift, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Lomentum, a cosmetic paste of bean-meal, smoothed a wrinkled belly before appearing in the bright light of the baths (Stephanus's baths named). Anchored to the named cosmetic; short answer supported verbatim (scisso... ventri).

pairs.source_text: Ebria nos madidis rumpit tibicina buccis: Saepe duas pariter, saepe monaulon habet.
pairs.question: Quot tibias pariter tibicina saepe inflat apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: How many pipes does the flute-girl often blow at once, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The tibicina of the banquet played the double pipe — two tibiae at once — or sometimes the single monaulos. A fact of Roman musical culture anchored to the named player and instrument; number answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid me conpactam ceris et harundine rides? Quae primum structa est fistula talis erat.
pairs.question: Quibus rebus fistula pastoricia conpacta est, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Of what is the shepherd's panpipe put together, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The fistula (panpipe, the syrinx) is reeds joined with wax — and, the couplet adds, the very first panpipe was just such. Anchored to the named instrument; two-noun answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Taurino poteras pectus constringere tergo: Nam pellis mammas non capit ista tuas.
pairs.question: Quo indumento pectus mulieris constringi solebat, quod mamillare vocatur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: With what garment was a woman's chest bound, the one called mamillare in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: A leather band (a band of skin).
pairs.derivation: The mamillare (the lemma) was a breast-band of leather; the joke offers bull's hide for a bust the ordinary skin band cannot hold. A named garment of daily dress; answer supported verbatim (pellis mammas non capit ista).

pairs.source_text: Lambere quae turpes prohibet tua prandia muscas, Alitis eximiae cauda superba fuit.
pairs.question: Ex cuius avis cauda fit muscarium quod muscas a prandio prohibet, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: From which bird's tail is made the fly-whisk that keeps flies off one's lunch, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The muscarium pavoninum (the lemma): fly-whisks at table were made from the proud tail of the peacock, the 'matchless bird.' Anchored to the named utensil; one-word answer supported by lemma + couplet (alitis eximiae cauda).

pairs.source_text: Peccantis famuli pugno ne percute dentes: Clara Rhodos coptam quam tibi misit edat.
pairs.question: Quae insula coptas, dura illa crustula, mittere solebat, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What island used to send the copta, that hard biscuit, as Martial jokes?
pairs.derivation: The copta Rhodiaca — the proverbially rock-hard biscuit from famous Rhodes (hard enough to punish a slave's teeth in place of a punch). Named food + named place; one-word answer supported verbatim (Clara Rhodos coptam... misit).

pairs.source_text: Si vis esse satur, nostrum potes esse Priapum: Ipsa licet rodas inguina, purus eris.
pairs.question: Cuius dei imago e siligine ficta inter dona Saturnalicia editur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: The image of what god, shaped from fine wheat flour, is eaten among the Saturnalian gifts in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The Priapus siligineus (the lemma): pastry-work in the shape of the god Priapus, of fine siligo flour, which one may eat entire and stay 'pure.' A named festive confection; answer supported by lemma + couplet (nostrum potes esse Priapum).

pairs.source_text: Iste tibi faciet bona Saturnalia porcus, Inter spumantes ilice pastus apros.
pairs.question: Quod animal bona Saturnalia facere dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What animal is said to make a good Saturnalia, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The pig — here acorn-fed among the boars — was the canonical Saturnalian feast animal (the porcus Saturnalicius). Festival + named animal; one-word answer supported verbatim (faciet bona Saturnalia porcus).

pairs.source_text: Qui venit botulus mediae tibi tempore brumae, Saturni septem venerat ante dies.
pairs.question: Quot dies Saturnalia durabant, ut testatur Martialis in Apophoretis?
pairs.question_en: How many days did the Saturnalia last, as Martial attests in the Apophoreta?
pairs.derivation: The botulus (sausage) arriving at midwinter had already come before, during 'the seven days of Saturn' — prime evidence that the Saturnalia of Martial's day ran seven days. Festival + number; answer supported verbatim (Saturni septem... dies).

pairs.source_text: Psittacus a vobis aliorum nomina discam: Hoc didici per me dicere CAESAR HAVE.
pairs.question: Quam salutationem psittacus ille per se dicere didicit apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What greeting did the parrot in Martial learn to say all by itself?
pairs.derivation: Talking parrots were taught greetings as luxury pets; this one learned unprompted to hail the emperor — a famous piece of imperial-age bird lore (cf. the raven of the Ara). Anchored to the parrot gift; short quoted answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Flet Philomela nefas incesti Tereos, et quae Muta puella fuit, garrula fertur avis.
pairs.question: In quam avem Philomela, quae muta puella fuerat, mutata fertur?
pairs.question_en: Into what bird is Philomela, who had been a mute girl, said to have been changed?
pairs.derivation: The Philomela myth in its Roman form: the girl silenced by Tereus becomes the garrulous singing bird — the luscinia (the lemma). The bird's identity as the nightingale is the epigram's subject; canonical shared myth, supported by lemma + couplet.

pairs.source_text: Pica loquax certa dominum te voce saluto: Si me non videas, esse negabis avem.
pairs.question: Quae avis loquax dominum certa voce salutare dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What talkative bird is said to greet its master with a distinct voice, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The talking magpie kept as a greeting pet — so human-voiced that unseen you would deny it is a bird. A named bird of Roman pet culture; one-word answer supported verbatim (Pica loquax... saluto).

pairs.source_text: Si tibi talis erit, qualem dilecta Catullo Lesbia plorabat, hic habitare potest.
pairs.question: Quae puella, Catullo dilecta, avem suam mortuam plorabat, ut memorat Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What girl, beloved of Catullus, wept for her dead bird, as Martial recalls?
pairs.derivation: The most famous pet bird of Latin literature — Lesbia's passer, mourned in Catullus's poems — invoked to size the ivory cage. Two named literary figures; one-word answer supported verbatim (dilecta Catullo Lesbia plorabat).

pairs.source_text: Artis ebur medicae narthecia cernis: habebis Munera, quae cuperet Paccius esse sua.
pairs.question: Cuius artis instrumentum est narthecium, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: Of what art is the narthecium (case for salves) the instrument, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The narthecium, here of ivory, was the physician's box of drugs and salves — a gift the (famous) doctor Paccius would covet. Named object + named profession; short answer supported verbatim (artis ebur medicae narthecia).

pairs.source_text: Ludite lascivi, sed tantum ludite, servi: Haec signata mihi quinque diebus erunt.
pairs.question: Quot diebus flagra signata iacebunt, dum Saturnalibus servi ludunt, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: For how many days will the whips lie sealed away while the slaves play at the Saturnalia, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: Saturnalian license for slaves: the whips are sealed up for the five days of the festival while the slaves play unpunished (Martial elsewhere counts seven days of Saturn; the couplet's own figure is five). Anchored to the flagra gift + the festival; number answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Invisae nimium pueris grataeque magistris, Clara Prometheo munere ligna sumus.
pairs.question: Cuius munere clara sunt ligna ferularum, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: By whose gift is the wood of the fennel-stalks (ferulae) famous, as Martial says?
pairs.answer_en: By Prometheus's (he carried the stolen fire in a fennel stalk).
pairs.derivation: The myth that Prometheus brought fire to men hidden in a fennel stalk (ferula) — 'famous for Prometheus's gift.' Named mythic figure + named plant; one-word answer supported verbatim (Clara Prometheo munere ligna).

pairs.source_text: Invisae nimium pueris grataeque magistris, Clara Prometheo munere ligna sumus.
pairs.question: Quibus invisae, quibus gratae erant ferulae in schola Romana, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: To whom were the ferulae (canes) hateful and to whom welcome in the Roman school, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: Hateful to the boys, welcome to the schoolmasters.
pairs.derivation: The ferula as the schoolmaster's instrument of punishment — the emblematic fact of Roman schooling (cf. Juvenal's 'manum ferulae subduximus'). Anchored to the named implement; paired answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: In pretio scopas testatur palma fuisse. Otia sed scopis nunc analecta dedit.
pairs.question: Ex qua arbore scopae Romanae fieri solebant, ut testatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: From what tree were Roman brooms usually made, as Martial attests?
pairs.derivation: Brooms (scopae) were made of palm fronds; the couplet adds that the crumb-collector (analecta) has now given brooms a rest. Named object + named material; short answer supported verbatim (scopas... palma).

pairs.source_text: Defendet manus haec scapulas mordente molesto Pulice, vel si quid pulice sordidius.
pairs.question: Cuius membri formam habebat scalptorium eboreum, quo scapulae a pulice defenduntur?
pairs.question_en: The shape of what limb did the ivory back-scratcher have, with which the shoulder-blades are defended from the flea?
pairs.derivation: The scalptorium (the lemma) was an ivory hand on a stick for scratching flea-bitten shoulders. A named toilette implement of daily life; one-word answer supported verbatim (Defendet manus haec scapulas).

pairs.source_text: Ne toga barbatos faciat vel paenula libros, Haec abies chartis tempora longa dabit.
pairs.question: Ex qua materia manuale, quod libros a tritu vestis defendit, factum erat apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Of what material was the manuale made, the case that protects books from the rubbing of one's clothes, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The manuale, a fir-wood case, kept the toga or paenula from fraying one's book-rolls 'bearded' and gave the papyrus long life. A named object of book culture; short answer supported verbatim (Haec abies chartis tempora longa dabit).

pairs.source_text: Nomina dat spondae pictis pulcherrima pinnis Nunc Iunonis avis, sed prius Argus erat.
pairs.question: Quis prius fuit pavo, avis Iunonis, ut narrat Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Who was the peacock, Juno's bird, before, as Martial relates?
pairs.derivation: The shared myth behind the peacock's eyed tail: Juno's bird was formerly Argus, her hundred-eyed guard, whose eyes she set in its feathers. Named goddess + named figure; one-word answer supported verbatim (Nunc Iunonis avis, sed prius Argus erat).

pairs.source_text: Accipe lunata scriptum testudine sigma. Octo capit; veniat quisquis amicus erit.
pairs.question: Quot convivas capit sigma, lectus ille lunatus, apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: How many diners does the sigma, the crescent-shaped couch, hold in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The sigma (stibadium), the crescent dining-couch named from the lunate Greek letter, here inlaid with tortoiseshell, seats eight. A named furnishing of the Roman dinner; number answer supported verbatim (Octo capit).

pairs.source_text: Femineam nobis cherson si credis inesse, Deciperis: pelagi mascula praeda sumus.
pairs.question: Ex qua testudine gustatorium pretiosum factum est, terrestri an marina, ut ipsum loquitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: From which tortoise is the costly hors-d'oeuvre tray made, the land or the sea one, as it says of itself in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Fine tortoiseshell ware came from the sea-turtle — the tray boasts it is 'the masculine prey of the deep,' not the land tortoise (cherson). Anchored to the named serving-piece; short answer supported verbatim (pelagi mascula praeda sumus).

pairs.source_text: Accipe felices, Atlantica munera, silvas: Aurea qui dederit dona, minora dabit.
pairs.question: Ex quibus silvis mensa citrea, munus pretiosissimum, petebatur, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: From what forests was the citrus-wood table, that most costly gift, sought, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Citrus-wood for luxury tables came from the Atlas region of Mauretania — 'Atlantic gifts.' Named object + named region; short answer supported verbatim (Atlantica munera, silvas).

pairs.source_text: Accipe felices, Atlantica munera, silvas: Aurea qui dederit dona, minora dabit.
pairs.question: Utrum maius munus dat, qui mensam citream an qui dona aurea dederit, secundum Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Who gives the greater gift, the man who gives a citrus-wood table or the man who gives gifts of gold, according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: The giver of the citrus-wood table.
pairs.derivation: The proverbial extravagance of citrus-wood tables: they outvalued gold itself ('he who gives golden gifts will give less'). Anchored to the named luxury; short comparative answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Puncta notis ilex et acuta cuspide clusa Saepe redemptoris prodere furta solet.
pairs.question: Cuius hominis furta quinquepedal prodere solet, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Whose frauds does the five-foot measuring rod usually expose, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The quinquepedal (the lemma), a five-foot rule of holm-oak marked with points, was the tool for catching a contractor (redemptor) cheating on measurements. Named instrument + named trade; one-word answer supported verbatim (redemptoris prodere furta).

pairs.source_text: Non est ista recens nec nostri gloria caeli: Primus in his Mentor, dum facit illa, bibit.
pairs.question: Quis artifex primus in poculis archetypis, dum ea facit, bibisse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What craftsman is said to have first drunk from the antique embossed cups while he was making them, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Mentor, the most celebrated Greek silver-chaser, byword for antique masterwork plate at Rome — the cups' pedigree is that Mentor himself first drank from them. Named artist; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nos sumus audacis plebeia toreumata vitri, Nostra neque ardenti gemma feritur aqua.
pairs.question: Qua re calices vitrei plebeii non feriuntur, ut ipsi gloriantur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: By what are the plebeian glass cups not cracked, as they themselves boast in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: By hot water (unlike precious crystal, hot drinks do not crack them).
pairs.derivation: Common glassware could take hot drinks that shattered precious crystal and murrine — the 'bold' cheap cups' one advantage. Anchored to the named ware; short answer supported verbatim (neque ardenti gemma feritur aqua).

pairs.source_text: Glorior arte magis: nam Myos iste labor.
pairs.question: Cuius artificis labor erat phiala aurea caelata, qua arte magis quam metallo gloriatur, apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Whose workmanship was the chased golden bowl, which glories more in its art than in its metal, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Mys, with Mentor a canonical Greek master-chaser; the bowl, though red with Callaician (Spanish) gold, boasts of his art more than the metal. Named artist + named gold-source; one-word answer supported verbatim (Myos iste labor).

pairs.source_text: Vilia sutoris calicem monimenta Vatini Accipe; sed nasus longior ille fuit.
pairs.question: Cuius artificii homo fuit Vatinius ille, a quo calices Vatinii nomen traxerunt?
pairs.question_en: Of what trade was that Vatinius from whom the Vatinian cups took their name?
pairs.derivation: The calices Vatinii, cheap long-nosed cups, were named for Vatinius the cobbler (of Beneventum, cf. Juvenal 5.46) — a piece of shared tableware lore. Named man + trade; one-word answer supported verbatim (sutoris... Vatini).

pairs.source_text: Grandia ne viola parvo chrysendeta mullo: Ut minimum, libras debet habere duas.
pairs.question: Quot libras mullus habere debet, qui in lance chrysendeta ponatur, ut praecipit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: How many pounds must a mullet weigh to be served on a gold-inlaid dish, as Martial prescribes?
pairs.derivation: The Roman obsession with mullet size: a fish worthy of the grand chrysendeta must weigh two pounds at minimum. Named dish + named fish + number; answer supported verbatim (Ut minimum, libras... duas).

pairs.source_text: Arretina nimis ne spernas vasa monemus: Lautus erat Tuscis Porsena fictilibus.
pairs.question: Quis rex Tuscis fictilibus lautus fuisse dicitur, ut monet Martialis de vasis Arretinis?
pairs.question_en: What king is said to have lived in style with Tuscan earthenware, as Martial notes of Arretine ware?
pairs.derivation: Arretium's famous red pottery defended by the example of Porsena, the Etruscan king, who was 'lautus' with Tuscan crockery. Named ware + named king; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Barbara de pictis veni bascauda Britannis; Sed me iam mavolt dicere Roma suam.
pairs.question: A qua gente bascauda Romam venit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: From what people did the bascauda (basket-work vessel) come to Rome, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The bascauda, a British import (the word itself Celtic) that Rome had adopted as her own — with the stock ethnographic epithet 'painted Britons.' Named object + named people; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si non ignotast docti tibi terra Catulli, Potasti testa Raetica vina mea.
pairs.question: Quae vina in terra docti Catulli e panaca bibuntur, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What wines are drunk from the panaca in the homeland of learned Catullus, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: Raetian wine belonged to the Verona country — 'the land of learned Catullus' — drunk from the local panaca jar; also attests Verona as Catullus's homeland. Named wine + named poet's country; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cum mihi boleti dederint tam nobile nomen, Prototomis - pudet heu! - servio coliculis.
pairs.question: A quo cibo boletaria nomen suum nobile acceperunt, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: From what food did the boletaria (mushroom-dishes) take their noble name, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The boletar was the dish named for the boletus, the noblest mushroom of the Roman table — though, it complains, it now serves cheap early-cut cabbage sprouts. Named dish + named food; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Accipe non vili calices de pulvere natos, Sed Surrentinae leve toreuma rotae.
pairs.question: Cuius loci rota calices fictiles nobiles tornavit, quos laudat Martialis?
pairs.question_en: The wheel of what place turned the fine clay cups that Martial praises?
pairs.derivation: Surrentine cups — the respected fine pottery of Surrentum on the bay of Naples, 'the smooth embossed work of the Surrentine wheel,' born of no cheap clay. Named place-product; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Setinos, moneo, nostra nive frange trientes: Pauperiore mero tingere lina potes.
pairs.question: Qua re Setinum merum frangi (temperari) monet colum nivarium apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: With what does the snow-strainer advise that Setine wine be 'broken' (tempered), in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Chilling wine through snow — the colum nivarium (snow-strainer) for the noble Setine, linen for cheaper stuff. Named wine + named practice; one-word answer supported verbatim (nostra nive frange trientes).

pairs.source_text: Frigida non deerit, non deerit calda petenti. Sed tu morosa ludere parce siti.
pairs.question: Quas duas aquas urceoli ministratorii convivae petenti praebent apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Which two waters do the serving-jugs supply to the diner who asks, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Roman table service offered both frigida and calda — cold water and the hot water for mixing with wine — from the ministering jugs. Named vessel + the two named drinks; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hic tibi donatur pansa ruber urceus ansa. Stoicus hoc gelidam Fronto petebat aquam.
pairs.question: Quis Stoicus gelidam aquam urceo fictili petebat, ut refert Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What Stoic used to fetch cold water in an earthenware jug, as Martial reports?
pairs.derivation: The red clay urceus dignified by philosophic frugality: the Stoic Fronto drank his cold water from just such a jug. Named philosopher + named vessel; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nos Satyri, nos Bacchus amat, nos ebria tigris, Perfusos domini lambere docta pedes.
pairs.question: Qui deus cum Satyris suis calathos amare dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What god, along with his Satyrs, is said to love the calathus cups, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The calathus as the Bacchic drinking-cup, loved by Bacchus, the Satyrs, and the god's drunken tigress taught to lick her master's wine-drenched feet. Named god + named cup; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quae non sollicitus teneat servetque minister, Sume Saguntino pocula facta luto.
pairs.question: Ex cuius oppidi luto pocula vilia facta sunt, quae minister sine sollicitudine tenet, apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: From the clay of what town are the cheap cups made that a servant can hold without anxiety, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Saguntine clay-ware, the inexpensive Spanish pottery a slave need not fear dropping — its cheapness the whole point of the gift. Named place-product; one-word answer supported verbatim (Saguntino... luto).

pairs.source_text: Gemmatum Scythicis ut luceat ignibus aurum, Aspice. Quot digitos exuit iste calix!
pairs.question: Quibus ignibus aurum calicum gemmatorum lucere dicit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: With what fires does Martial say the gold of the jeweled cups gleams?
pairs.answer_en: With Scythian fires (the green gems, emeralds, of Scythia).
pairs.derivation: Jeweled gold cups set with 'Scythian fires' — the smaragdi (emeralds) proverbially from Scythia — gems stripped, the couplet jokes, from many fingers' rings. Named gem-source; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si caldum potas, ardenti murra Falerno Convenit et melior fit sapor inde mero.
pairs.question: Quod poculum ardenti Falerno caldo maxime convenit, ita ut melior fiat sapor, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What cup best suits blazing-hot Falernian, so that the flavor of the wine actually improves, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The famous murrine ware: it tolerated hot drinks and was believed to improve the wine's flavor — here paired with hot Falernian. Named ware + named wine; short answer supported verbatim (murra Falerno convenit... melior fit sapor).

pairs.source_text: Hanc tibi Cumano rubicundam pulvere testam Municipem misit casta Sibylla suam.
pairs.question: Quae vates patellam Cumanam, municipem suam, misisse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What prophetess is said to have sent the Cumaean dish, her fellow-townswoman, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Cumae's red earthenware personified as fellow-citizen of the Cumaean Sibyl — attesting both the town's red pottery and the Sibyl's famous residence there. Named place + named prophetess; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Aspicis ingenium Nili: quibus addere plura Dum cupit, a quotiens perdidit auctor opus!
pairs.question: Cuius fluminis ingenium in calicibus vitreis agnoscitur, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: The ingenuity of what river is recognized in the glass cups, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Fine glassware as 'the ingenuity of the Nile' — Egypt (Alexandria) was the famed center of glass craft, whose artists often ruined a piece by attempting one touch more. Named river-region; one-word answer supported verbatim (ingenium Nili).

pairs.source_text: Non potare nivem, sed aquam potare recentem De nive commenta est ingeniosa sitis.
pairs.question: Quid ex lagona nivaria potatur, nix ipsa an aqua, ut docet Martialis?
pairs.answer: Aqua recens de nive (non ipsa nix).
pairs.question_en: What is drunk from the snow-flask, the snow itself or water, as Martial explains?
pairs.answer_en: Fresh water chilled by the snow (not the snow itself).
pairs.derivation: The refinement of Roman cold drinks: ingenious thirst devised drinking not melted snow but fresh water cooled through snow. Anchored to the lagona nivaria (the lemma); short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Massiliae fumos miscere nivalibus undis Parce, puer, constet ne tibi pluris aqua.
pairs.question: Cuius urbis vina 'fumos' appellat Martialis?
pairs.question_en: The wines of what city does Martial call 'smoke'?
pairs.derivation: Massilia's cheap wine, aged in smoke, was proverbially 'fumus' — not worth mixing with snow-cooled water that costs more than it. Named city + its wine's byname; one-word answer supported verbatim (Massiliae fumos).

pairs.source_text: Dum poscor crepitu digitorum et verna moratur, O quotiens paelex culcita facta mea est!
pairs.question: Quo signo matella nocte a domino poscebatur, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: By what signal was the chamber-pot called for at night by its master, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: By a snapping of the fingers.
pairs.derivation: The Roman custom of snapping one's fingers to summon the slave with the matella (chamber-pot) — with the joke that when the boy dallies, the mattress plays rival. Named object + named gesture; short answer supported verbatim (poscor crepitu digitorum).

pairs.source_text: Sum cocleis habilis, sed nec minus utilis ovis. Numquid scis, potius cur cocleare vocer?
pairs.question: Quibus duobus cibis cocleare aptum est, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: For which two foods is the cocleare (pointed spoon) suited, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The cocleare, the small pointed spoon named from the snail (coclea), served for snails and equally for eggs — the two shell-foods of the Roman table. Named utensil; two-noun answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Romanos rerum dominos gentemque togatam Ille facit, magno qui dedit astra patri.
pairs.question: Quo epitheto a veste sua gens Romana appellatur, quod ex Vergilio refert Martialis in Apophoretis?
pairs.question_en: By what epithet, drawn from its dress, is the Roman race called, which Martial in the Apophoreta echoes from Vergil?
pairs.derivation: The toga as the Roman national dress: Martial quotes Vergil's famous line (Aen. 1.282) 'Romanos rerum dominos gentemque togatam' on the gift of a toga. Anchored to Romans + toga; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si matutinos facilest tibi perdere somnos, Attrita veniet sportula saepe toga.
pairs.question: Quid clienti, qui matutinos somnos perdere sustinet, cum attrita toga saepe veniet, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What will often come, along with a worn-out toga, to the client who can bear to lose his morning sleep, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The client system in one couplet: rise before dawn, wear out your toga at the salutatio, and earn the sportula. Named institution + named garment; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Gallia Santonico vestit te bardocucullo. Cercopithecorum paenula nuper erat.
pairs.question: Quae terra homines bardocucullo Santonico vestit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What land clothes men with the Santonic bardocucullus (hooded cloak), on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The bardocucullus, the hooded cloak of the Gallic Santones (whence 'Santonic'), a Gaulish export garment at Rome. Named garment + named land and people; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Roma magis fuscis vestitur, Gallia rufis, Et placet hic pueris militibusque colos.
pairs.question: Quo colore lanarum Roma, quo Gallia magis vestitur, secundum Martialem?
pairs.question_en: In wool of what color does Rome mostly dress, and in what color Gaul, according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: Rome in dark (brown), Gaul in red.
pairs.derivation: The color-geography of dress: Rome wore the dark Canusian wools, Gaul the red — and red, Martial adds, pleases boys and soldiers. Two named places + colors; paired answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ingrediare viam caelo licet usque sereno, Ad subitas numquam scortea desit aquas.
pairs.question: Ad quas res paenula scortea viatori semper praesto esse debet, ut monet Martialis?
pairs.question_en: For what should the traveler always have his leather paenula at hand, as Martial advises?
pairs.derivation: The scortea, the leather rain-cloak of the Roman traveler: carry it even under a clear sky against sudden showers. Named garment; short answer supported verbatim (Ad subitas... scortea... aquas).

pairs.source_text: Si veneto prasinove faves, quid coccina sumes? Ne fias ista transfuga sorte, vide.
pairs.question: Quibus duabus factionibus circensium favere spectatores solitos innuit Martialis de lacernis coccineis?
pairs.question_en: Which two circus factions does Martial imply the spectators usually favor, in the couplet on scarlet cloaks?
pairs.derivation: The great chariot factions of the circus — venetus (Blue) and prasinus (Green): wearing scarlet, you would look like a deserter of your color. Named factions; two-word answer supported verbatim (veneto prasinove faves).

pairs.source_text: Non est lana mihi mendax, nec mutor aheno. Sic placeant Tyriae: me mea tinxit ovis.
pairs.question: Unde colorem suum habent lacernae Baeticae, ut ipsae apud Martialem gloriantur?
pairs.answer: A sua ove (natura lanae, non fuco).
pairs.question_en: From what do the Baetic cloaks get their color, as they themselves boast in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: From their own sheep (the wool's natural color, not dye).
pairs.derivation: The famous naturally-colored (golden-brown) wool of Baetica in Spain: no lying wool, no dye-vat — 'my own sheep dyed me,' unlike Tyrian purple. Named region-product; short answer supported verbatim (me mea tinxit ovis).

pairs.source_text: Amphitheatrali nos commendamus ab usu, Cum teget algentes alba lacerna togas.
pairs.question: Quo in spectaculo lacerna alba super togam sumi solebat, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: At what spectacle was the white lacerna worn over the toga, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The white lacerna as amphitheater dress, worn over the chilly toga at the games (white was the required color of the spectator's cloak under Domitian). Named garment + named venue; short answer supported verbatim (amphitheatrali... usu).

pairs.source_text: Nec fora sunt nobis nec sunt vadimonia nota: Hoc opus est, pictis accubuisse toris.
pairs.question: Quod unum opus est vestis cenatoriae, ut ipsa loquitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What is the one business of dinner-clothes, as they say of themselves in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: To recline on the embroidered dining-couches.
pairs.derivation: The cenatoria: a distinct outfit worn only for dining — it knows neither forum nor court-dates, its sole work is reclining at table. Named garment-class; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nobilius villosa tegant tibi lintea citrum: Orbibus in nostris circulus esse potest.
pairs.question: Qualem mensam lintea villosa (mantelia) tegere debent apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What sort of table should the shaggy linen cloths (mantelia) cover, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Tablecloths guarded the precious citrus tabletops — a wine-cup's ring may sit on the cloth, not the wood. Named textile + named luxury table; one-word answer supported verbatim (villosa tegant... lintea citrum).

pairs.source_text: Non hos lana dedit, sed olentis barba mariti: Cinyphio poterit planta latere sinu.
pairs.question: Ex qua materia udones Cilicii facti sunt, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: Of what material are Cilician udones (foot-socks) made, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Cilician cloth (cilicium) was woven of goat hair — the socks come 'not from wool but from the beard of the smelly husband' of the she-goats, of Cinyphian (North African) goat fleece. Named product; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dum toga per quinas gaudet requiescere luces, Hos poteris cultus sumere iure tuo.
pairs.question: Per quot dies toga Saturnalibus requiescit, dum synthesis iure sumitur, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: For how many days does the toga rest at the Saturnalia, while the synthesis is worn by right, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The synthesis (the lemma) as the licensed Saturnalian dress: while the toga 'delights to rest for five days,' one may wear the dinner-suit by right. Named garments + festival + number; answer supported verbatim (per quinas... luces).

pairs.source_text: Vellera consumunt Patavinae multa trilices, Et pingues tunicas serra secare potest.
pairs.question: Cuius urbis tunicae trilices tam pingues erant ut serra secari possent, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Of what city were the triple-twill tunics so thick that a saw could cut them, as Martial jokes?
pairs.derivation: Patavium's famous heavy woolens: its trilix (triple-woven) tunics consume masses of fleece and are thick enough for the saw. Named city-product; one-word answer supported verbatim (Patavinae... trilices).

pairs.source_text: Haec tibi Memphitis tellus dat munera: victa est Pectine Niliaco iam Babylonos acus.
pairs.question: Cuius urbis acus pectine Niliaco victa esse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: The needle of what city is said to have been beaten by the Nile's comb (loom), in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The two famed textile arts compared: Egyptian polymita weaving (the 'comb of the Nile') has now surpassed Babylonian embroidery ('the needle of Babylon'). Two named centers; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Lodices mittet docti tibi terra Catulli: Nos Helicaonia de regione sumus.
pairs.question: Quae terra lodices mittere solet, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What land customarily sends the lodices (blankets), as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: Verona — 'the land of learned Catullus' — was known for its lodices (blankets), while the square gausapum speaks as a native of Patavium ('the region of Helicaon'). Named region-product; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ebria Sidoniae cum sim de sanguine conchae, Non video, quare sobria lana vocer.
pairs.question: Cuius conchae sanguine lanae amethystinae tinguntur, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: With the blood of what shellfish are the amethyst-colored wools dyed, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: Amethystine wool was dyed with the Phoenician murex — 'drunk with the blood of the Sidonian shell' (the couplet then puns on amethystos, 'unintoxicated'). Named dye-source; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Velleribus primis Apulia, Parma secundis Nobilis; Altinum tertia laudat ovis.
pairs.question: Quae terra velleribus primis, quae secundis, quod oppidum tertiis nobile est, secundum Martialem?
pairs.answer: Apulia primis, Parma secundis, Altinum tertiis.
pairs.question_en: What land is famed for the first-rank fleeces, which for the second, and what town for the third, according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: Apulia first, Parma second, Altinum third.
pairs.derivation: The canonical ranking of Italian white wools: Apulia first, Parma second, Altinum third — the ambient market knowledge of Roman wool (cf. Pliny and Columella on the same trio). Three named places; ranked answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nos Lacedaemoniae pastor donavit amicae: Deterior Ledae purpura matris erat.
pairs.question: Quis pastor lanas Tyrias Lacedaemoniae amicae donavisse fingitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What shepherd is imagined in Martial to have given the Tyrian purple wool to his Spartan mistress?
pairs.derivation: The mythic pedigree of Tyrian wool: 'the shepherd' who gave it to his 'Lacedaemonian mistress' is Paris giving to Helen — confirmed by 'her mother Leda' in the pentameter. Decoding the periphrasis is exactly the shared myth-knowledge the couplet assumes; supported by the quoted lines.

pairs.source_text: Non tantum pullo lugentes vellere lanas, Sed solet et calices haec dare terra suos.
pairs.question: Quibus duabus mercibus terra Pollentina nobilis erat, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: For which two wares was the land of Pollentia known, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: For dark (mourning) wools and for its cups.
pairs.derivation: Pollentia (the lemma: lanae Pollentinae) supplied both the dark 'mourning' fleeces and its own dark pottery cups. Named town + two products; two-noun answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tomentum concisa palus Circense vocatur. Haec pro Leuconico stramina pauper emit.
pairs.question: Quod tomentum pauper pro Leuconico emere solet, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What mattress-stuffing does the poor man buy in place of the Leuconian, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The rich/poor bedding pair: chopped marsh-reed was sold as 'tomentum Circense,' the poor man's substitute for the fine Leuconian shorn-wool flock. Two named stuffings; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Lassus Amyclaea poteris requiescere pluma, Interior cycni quam tibi lana dedit.
pairs.question: Cuius avis pluma interior culcitas mollissimas implebat, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: The inner down of what bird filled the softest pillows, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The finest bedding was stuffed with swan's down — 'the inner wool of the swan,' called Amyclaean after the swan of Leda's Amyclae. Named bird-product; one-word answer supported verbatim (Interior cycni... lana).

pairs.source_text: Redde pilam: sonat aes thermarum. Ludere pergis? Virgine vis sola lotus abire domum.
pairs.question: Quo signo lusores pilae in thermas vocabantur, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: By what signal were the ball-players summoned to the hot baths, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: By the sounding bronze (the bell of the baths).
pairs.derivation: The bell (tintinabulum, the lemma) rang to announce the thermae were open — time to give up the ball, or wash at home in the cold Aqua Virgo alone. A named institution of bath life; answer supported verbatim (sonat aes thermarum).

pairs.source_text: Reddidit Eurydicen vati: sed perdidit ipse, Dum sibi non credit nec patienter amat.
pairs.question: Quam uxorem cithara vati Orpheo reddidit, quam ipse mox iterum perdidit?
pairs.question_en: What wife did the lyre restore to the bard Orpheus, whom he himself soon lost again?
pairs.derivation: The Orpheus myth on the gift of a cithara: the lyre won Eurydice back from the underworld, but the bard lost her by not trusting himself and looking back. Canonical shared story; one-word answer supported verbatim (Reddidit Eurydicen vati... perdidit ipse).

pairs.source_text: Fervida ne trito tibi pollice pusula surgat, Exornent docilem candida plectra lyram.
pairs.question: Cui digito plectrum parcit, ne pusula fervida surgat, dum lyra pulsatur, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: Which finger does the plectrum spare from raising a burning blister when the lyre is struck, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The plectrum's practical point: it saves the player's thumb, worn and blistered by plucking the strings bare. Named implement + named finger; one-word answer supported verbatim (trito... pollice pusula).

pairs.source_text: Garrulus in laxo cur anulus orbe vagatur? Cedat ut argutis obvia turba trochis.
pairs.question: Quam ob rem anuli garruli in orbe trochi currentis vagantur, ut docet Martialis?
pairs.question_en: For what purpose do jingling rings run loose on the hoop's rim, as Martial explains?
pairs.answer_en: So that the crowd in the way may step aside for the hoops.
pairs.derivation: The trochus, the boys' driving-hoop, carried loose metal rings whose jingle warned pedestrians to clear the way — the purpose is stated, not left to interpretation. Named toy; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Haec illi sine sorte datur, cui nomina Rhenus Vera dedit. Deciens adde Falerna, puer.
pairs.question: Quod flumen Domitiano nomina vera, id est Germanici cognomen, dedisse ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What river does Martial say gave Domitian his 'true name' — the surname Germanicus?
pairs.derivation: The golden Victory goes without lot to him 'to whom the Rhine gave his true name' — Domitian, styled Germanicus after his Rhine (Chattan) campaign. Named river + imperial cognomen; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Gloria tam parvi non est obscura sigilli: Istius pueri Brutus amator erat.
pairs.question: Quis amator erat pueri illius, sigilli celeberrimi, ut refert Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Who was the lover (devotee) of that famous boy-statuette, as Martial reports?
pairs.derivation: The 'puer Bruti,' the celebrated small bronze boy that Brutus so loved it bore his name — a stock piece of Roman art lore (Martial cites it elsewhere too). Named collector + named statuette; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ad te reptanti, puer insidiose, lacertae Parce: cupit digitis illa perire tuis.
pairs.question: Quod animal puer ille insidiosus in signo Sauroctono petit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What creature does the lurking boy stalk in the Sauroctonos statue, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The Sauroctonos ('lizard-slayer'), the famous statue type of the boy (Apollo, after Praxiteles) poised to kill the creeping lizard — here in Corinthian bronze. Named artwork; one-word answer supported verbatim (reptanti... lacertae).

pairs.source_text: Flectit ab inviso morientia lumina disco Oebalius, Phoebi culpa dolorque, puer.
pairs.question: Quo instrumento Hyacinthus, Phoebi culpa dolorque, periit, ut pingitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: By what implement did Hyacinthus, Phoebus's fault and grief, die, as painted in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The Hyacinthus myth: the Spartan ('Oebalian') boy killed by the discus, the guilt and grief of Apollo who threw it — the painting shows him turning his dying eyes from the hated discus. Canonical myth; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Masculus intravit fontis, emersit utrumque: Pars est una patris, cetera matris habet.
pairs.question: Qualis fontem intravit Hermaphroditus et qualis emersit, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: In what form did Hermaphroditus enter the spring, and in what form did he emerge, as Martial says?
pairs.answer_en: He entered male and came out of both sexes.
pairs.derivation: The Hermaphroditus myth (Salmacis's spring): he went in a male and emerged double-natured, 'one part of his father, the rest of his mother' (Hermes and Aphrodite). Canonical shared story on the marble statue; answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cur a te pretium Danae, regnator Olympi, Accepit, gratis si tibi Leda dedit?
pairs.question: Quae femina Iovi gratis se dedisse dicitur, cum Danae pretium acceperit, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Which woman is said to have given herself to Jupiter for free, whereas Danae took a price, as Martial jokes?
pairs.derivation: Two canonical loves of Jupiter set side by side: Danae 'paid' with the golden shower, Leda (visited as the swan) gave gratis. Two named mythic women + the god; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sum figuli lusus russi persona Batavi. Quae tu derides, haec timet ora puer.
pairs.question: Cuius gentis ora russa persona illa fictilis refert, quam puer timet, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: The red face of what people does that clay mask represent, which a boy fears, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The persona Germana: a potter's clay mask with the red(-haired) Batavian face — the adult laughs, the child is frightened. The red Batavian is the stock ethnographic image; one-word answer supported verbatim (russi persona Batavi).

pairs.source_text: Elidit geminos infans nec respicit anguis. Iam poterat teneras hydra timere manus.
pairs.question: Quot anguis Hercules infans elisit, ut in signo Corinthio ostenditur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: How many snakes did the infant Hercules crush, as shown in the Corinthian bronze in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The canonical infant-Hercules scene: the baby strangling the two snakes sent against him, so that already the hydra might fear his tender hands. Named hero (lemma: Hercules Corinthius); number answer supported verbatim (geminos... anguis).

pairs.source_text: Dic mihi, virgo ferox, cum sit tibi cassis et hasta, Quare non habeas aegida. 'Caesar habet.'
pairs.question: Quis aegida Minervae habere dicitur, cum ipsa cassidem et hastam gerat, apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to hold Minerva's aegis, while she herself carries helmet and spear, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Domitian's special devotion to Minerva, his patron goddess: the silver statuette has helmet and spear, and the aegis 'Caesar has.' Named goddess + emperor; short answer supported verbatim ('Caesar habet').

pairs.source_text: Mutari melius tauro, pater optime divum, Tunc poteras, Io cum tibi vacca fuit.
pairs.question: In quod animal Iuppiter propter Europam mutatus est, ut pingitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Into what animal did Jupiter change for Europa, as painted in Martial?
pairs.derivation: On the painted Europa (the lemma): Jupiter became a bull to carry her off — the joke adds he should have done it when Io was his cow. Named god + named girl; short answer supported by lemma + couplet (mutari... tauro).

pairs.source_text: Clamabat tumidis audax Leandros in undis: 'Mergite me, fluctus, cum rediturus ero.'
pairs.question: Quando se mergi a fluctibus Leandros audax patiebatur, ut clamabat apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: When was bold Leander willing to be drowned by the waves, as he cried out in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: On his way back (spare me going, drown me returning).
pairs.derivation: The Leander story — the youth who swam the Hellespont nightly to his love — in Martial's famous epigrammatic point: drown me when I am returning, not going. Named hero; short answer supported verbatim (Mergite me... cum rediturus ero).

pairs.source_text: Ebrius haec fecit terris, puto, monstra Prometheus: Saturnalicio lusit et ipse luto.
pairs.question: Quis homines e luto finxisse fertur, ut iocatur Martialis de sigillo gibberi?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have fashioned mankind out of clay, as Martial jokes about the hunchback figurine?
pairs.derivation: The shared myth that Prometheus molded men from clay, turned into a joke: hunchbacks must be the work of a drunken Prometheus playing, like the potters, with 'Saturnalian clay' (the clay sigillaria given at the festival). Named figure; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Perlege Maeonio cantatas carmine ranas Et frontem nugis solvere disce meis.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae carmine ranae illae cantatae sunt, quas Batrachomachia narrat?
pairs.question_en: By the song of what poet were those frogs sung which the Batrachomachia tells of?
pairs.derivation: The Batrachomachia (the lemma), the mock-epic battle of the frogs, went under Homer's name — 'frogs sung in Maeonian song' (Maeonius = Homeric). Named work + author; short answer supported by lemma + verbatim epithet.

pairs.source_text: Ilias et Priami regnis inimicus Ulixes Multiplici pariter condita pelle latent.
pairs.question: Quae duo carmina Homeri in una membrana multiplici pariter condita sunt apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Which two poems of Homer are stored together in one many-folded parchment in Martial?
pairs.answer_en: The Iliad and the Odyssey (the poem of Ulysses).
pairs.derivation: The whole of Homer in a single parchment codex — the Iliad and 'Ulysses, enemy of Priam's kingdom' (the Odyssey in periphrasis) hidden together in the folded skin. A landmark of book history; answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Accipe facundi Culicem, studiose, Maronis, Ne nucibus positis ARMA VIRUMQUE legas.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae est Culex ille libellus, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: Of what poet is the little work called the Culex, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The Culex ('The Gnat') circulated as a light juvenile poem of Vergil — fit for the Saturnalia, so that 'with the nuts put away' one need not start Arma virumque (the Aeneid). Named work + author; short answer supported verbatim (Culicem... Maronis).

pairs.source_text: Quam brevis inmensum cepit membrana Maronem! Ipsius vultus prima tabella gerit.
pairs.question: Quid prima tabella membranarum Vergilium totum continentium gerit, ut miratur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What does the first leaf of the parchment codex containing the whole of Vergil carry, as Martial marvels?
pairs.derivation: The parchment pocket-Vergil with an author-portrait on its first page — 'how small a parchment has held immense Maro!' A famous document of early codex culture; answer supported verbatim (Ipsius vultus prima tabella gerit).

pairs.source_text: Hac primum iuvenum lascivos lusit amores; Nec Glycera pueri, Thais amica fuit.
pairs.question: Qua fabula Menander primum lascivos iuvenum amores lusisse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: With what play is Menander said in Martial to have first sported with the wanton loves of the young?
pairs.derivation: Menander's Thais (the Greek lemma) as the play with which he first treated young men's love-affairs — and Thais, not Glycera, was the young man's mistress. Named playwright + named play; one-word answer supported by lemma + couplet.

pairs.source_text: Si comes ista tibi fuerit membrana, putato Carpere te longas cum Cicerone vias.
pairs.question: Cuius auctoris membrana comes longarum viarum fingitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: The parchment codex of what author is imagined as the companion of long journeys, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Cicero in a parchment travel-codex: carry it and think yourself journeying with Cicero himself — the portability of the membrana is the very point of the gift. Named author; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cynthia - facundi carmen iuvenale Properti - Accepit famam, non minus ipsa dedit.
pairs.question: Quae puella carmine iuvenali Properti, quod Monobyblos vocatur, celebratur?
pairs.question_en: What girl is celebrated in the youthful poetry of Propertius, the book called Monobyblos?
pairs.derivation: Propertius's first book (the Monobyblos, the lemma) and its subject Cynthia, who 'received fame and gave no less' — the canonical elegiac pairing of poet and beloved. Named poet + named puella; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Pellibus exiguis artatur Livius ingens, Quem mea non totum bibliotheca capit.
pairs.question: Quis historicus ingens pellibus exiguis artari dicitur, quem tota bibliotheca non capit, apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What immense historian is said to be compressed into scanty skins, whom a whole library cannot hold, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated couplet on the parchment Livy: the huge history (142 books) squeezed into a small parchment codex, though Martial's own library cannot hold the whole. Named author; one-word answer supported verbatim (Pellibus exiguis artatur Livius ingens).

pairs.source_text: Hic erit, ut perhibent doctorum corda virorum, Primus Romana Crispus in historia.
pairs.question: Quis primus in Romana historia habetur, ut perhibent docti apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Who is held first in Roman historiography, as the learned declare in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The shared literary verdict, explicitly attributed to 'the hearts of learned men': Crispus (Sallust) ranks first in Roman history-writing. Named author + attributed judgment; short answer supported verbatim (Primus Romana Crispus in historia).

pairs.source_text: Haec tibi, multiplici quae structa est massa tabella, Carmina Nasonis quinque decemque gerit.
pairs.question: Quot carmina (libros) Metamorphosis Nasonis gerit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: How many poems (books) of Naso's Metamorphoses does the codex carry, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The Metamorphoses of Ovid in fifteen books, here stacked as a mass of many leaves in a parchment codex. Named work + author + number; answer supported verbatim (Carmina Nasonis quinque decemque).

pairs.source_text: Ussit amatorem Nemesis lasciva Tibullum, In tota iuvit quem nihil esse domo.
pairs.question: Quae puella amatorem Tibullum ussisse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What girl is said to have set the lover Tibullus aflame, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Nemesis, the beloved of Tibullus's second book of elegies — the canonical poet-and-mistress pairing (the pentameter echoes Tibullus's own line). Named poet + named puella; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sunt quidam, qui me dicant non esse poetam: Sed qui me vendit bybliopola putat.
pairs.question: Quis Lucanum poetam esse putat, cum quidam id negent, ut ipse iocatur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Who does think Lucan a poet, though some deny it, as the book itself jokes in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The ancient critical dispute whether Lucan was a 'poet' (or a versifying historian), answered commercially: his bookseller thinks so. Named author (lemma: Lucanus) + the book trade; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tantum magna suo debet Verona Catullo, Quantum parva suo Mantua Vergilio.
pairs.question: Cui poetae suo tantum debet Verona quantum Mantua Vergilio, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: To which poet of her own does Verona owe as much as Mantua owes to Vergil, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The paired hometown facts of Latin poetry: Catullus of Verona, Vergil of Mantua — great Verona owes the one what little Mantua owes the other. Two named poets + two named towns; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hic brevis ad numeros rapidum qui colligit unguem, Venit ab auriferis gentibus Astur equus.
pairs.question: A quibus gentibus venit asturco, equus brevis qui ad numeros gradum colligit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: From what peoples comes the asturco, the small horse that gathers its step to a rhythm, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: From the Astures, the gold-bearing peoples (of northern Spain).
