pairs.derivation: The asturco, the ambling pony that paces 'to a measure,' came from Asturia — whose peoples were proverbially gold-bearing (the Asturian mines). Named breed + named people; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Non sibi, sed domino venatur vertragus acer, Inlaesum leporem qui tibi dente feret.
pairs.question: Qualem leporem vertragus domino suo dente refert, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: In what condition does the vertragus (greyhound) carry the hare back to its master in its teeth, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The vertragus, the Celtic gazehound: it hunts for its master, not itself, retrieving the hare unhurt in its mouth — the defining virtue of the breed. Named dog (Celtic loanword); one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Callidus emissas eludere simius hastas, Si mihi cauda foret, cercopithecus eram.
pairs.question: Quid simio deest quo cercopithecus sit, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What does the ape lack that would make it a cercopithecus, as Martial jokes?
pairs.derivation: The Roman monkey taxonomy: the simius (ape, here trained to dodge thrown spears) is tailless; with a tail it would be a cercopithecus ('tail-ape'). Two named animals; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Aera Celaenaeos lugentia matris amores Esuriens Gallus vendere saepe solet.
pairs.question: Quis esuriens cymbala Matris deum vendere saepe solet, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What starving figure often sells the cymbals of the Mother of the gods, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: The Gallus (the begging priest of Cybele).
pairs.derivation: The cymbals of Cybele's cult — 'bronzes mourning the Mother's Celaenaean love' (Attis of Celaenae) — hawked by the hungry Gallus, her mendicant eunuch priest. Named cult figure + instrument; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sume Cytheriaco medicatum nectare ceston: Ussit amatorem balteus iste Iovem.
pairs.question: Cuius deae cestos, balteus amoris, etiam Iovem amatorem ussit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: The cestus, love's girdle of what goddess, set even Jupiter aflame as a lover, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Venus's cestus — the love-charming girdle of Homer's Iliad 14, steeped in 'Cytherean nectar' — which inflamed Jupiter himself. Named goddess + god; short answer supported verbatim (Cytheriaco... ceston... Iovem).

pairs.source_text: Currant verba licet, manus est velocior illis: Nondum lingua suum, dextra peregit opus.
pairs.question: Utra velocior est apud notarium, lingua an manus, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Which is quicker in the shorthand-writer, the tongue or the hand, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The notarius and Roman shorthand (notae): though the words race, the hand outruns them — the right hand finishes before the tongue. Named profession; short answer supported verbatim (manus est velocior illis).

pairs.source_text: Levis ab aequorea cortex Mareotica concha Fiat: inoffensa curret harundo via.
pairs.question: Quo instrumento charta Mareotica levigatur, ut calamus inoffensa via currat, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: With what implement is Mareotic papyrus polished smooth, so that the reed pen may run unimpeded, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Papyrus-finishing: the Egyptian (Mareotic) sheet was burnished with a smooth shell so the pen would not catch. A concrete fact of Roman book production; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Haec, quae saepe solet vinci, quae vincere raro, Parma tibi, scutum pumilionis erit.
pairs.question: Cui homini parma pro scuto erit, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: For what man will the parma (small shield) serve as a full scutum, as Martial jokes?
pairs.derivation: The parma was the small shield (of the Thraex, 'often beaten, rarely winning' — the parmularii Domitian disfavored), the scutum the large one: to a dwarf the parma is a scutum. Two named shield types; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dic mihi simpliciter, comoedis et citharoedis, Fibula, quid praestas? 'Carius ut futuant.'
pairs.question: Quibus artificibus scaenicis fibula imponi solebat, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: On what performers was the fibula (the performer's pin) customarily put, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The fibula, the infibulation pin worn by stage performers and singers (ostensibly to preserve the voice) — the couplet names its two wearers, comoedi and citharoedi. Named practice + professions; two-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Non tantum calamis, sed cantu fallitur ales, Callida dum tacita crescit harundo manu.
pairs.question: Quibus duabus rebus auceps alitem fallit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: By what two means does the fowler deceive the bird, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: Roman fowling technique: the bird is tricked by the limed reeds and by imitated song, while the jointed rod 'grows' silently in the fowler's hand toward the perch. Named craft; two-noun answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Praedo fuit volucrum: famulus nunc aucupis idem Decipit et captas non sibi maeret aves.
pairs.question: Cuius famulus factus est accipiter, qui aves iam non sibi capit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: Whose servant has the hawk become, now catching birds no longer for itself, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The trained hunting hawk — once a robber of birds, now the fowler's servant, grieving over catches not its own: early Roman evidence for hawking. Named bird + named craft; one-word answer supported verbatim (famulus nunc aucupis).

pairs.source_text: Dic quotus et quanti cupias cenare, nec unum Addideris verbum: cena parata tibi est.
pairs.question: Quae duo obsonatori dicenda sunt, ut cena statim paretur, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What two things must one tell the obsonator (caterer) for dinner to be made ready at once, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.answer_en: How many you dine and at what price (party size and budget).
pairs.derivation: The obsonator, the professional dinner-buyer: state the number of diners and the spend, add not one word more, and the cena is ready. Named profession; two-item answer supported verbatim (quotus et quanti cupias cenare).

pairs.source_text: Non satis est ars sola coco: servire palatum Nolo: cocus domini debet habere gulam.
pairs.question: Quid cocus praeter artem habere debet, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What must a cook have besides his skill, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The dictum on the Roman cook: skill alone is not enough — the cook must have his master's gula, cooking to the master's taste. Attributed saying with a checkable point; short answer supported verbatim (cocus domini debet habere gulam).

pairs.source_text: Rara tibi curva craticula sudet ofella; Spumeus in longa cuspide fumet aper.
pairs.question: Quod animal in longa cuspide (veribus) fumat, dum ofella in craticula sudat, apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: What animal smokes on the long spit while the morsel of pork sweats on the gridiron, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: Roman kitchen gear in one couplet: the curved craticula (gridiron) for the ofella (little chop), the long spit (verua, the lemma) for the whole foaming boar. Named implements + named dishes; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Mille tibi dulces operum manus ista figuras Extruet: huic uni parca laborat apis.
pairs.question: Cui uni artifici apis parca laborare dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: For which one craftsman alone is the thrifty bee said to labor, in Martial?
pairs.derivation: The pistor dulciarius (the lemma), the confectioner who builds a thousand sweet shapes: honey being the Roman sweetener, the bee works for him alone. Named trade; short answer supported by lemma + couplet (huic uni... laborat apis).

pairs.source_text: Surgite: iam vendit pueris ientacula pistor Cristataeque sonant undique lucis aves.
pairs.question: Quibus pistor ientacula prima luce vendere solet, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: To whom does the baker sell breakfasts at first light, on Martial's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The closing couplet of the Apophoreta: at cockcrow the baker is already selling ientacula (breakfasts — the adipata, lard-pastries of the lemma) to the boys on their way to school. Named meal + named trade; one-word answer supported verbatim.
